Eli climbs everything in sight: the couch back, the bookshelf, his crib rail. I'd like his new room ready for bedtime tonight. The dresser we're moving in is a 48-inch-tall five-drawer chest, and we have no wall anchors.

The move itself has been a bit of a saga. We're swapping rooms because the old nursery gets afternoon sun that makes it too warm, and the former office has a closet big enough for a proper toy bin and a reading nook. I've spent the last week repainting the walls a pale green that looked much more cheerful in the store, and my husband assembled a bed rail and a small bookshelf on Saturday with only one trip to the hardware store, which is a record. The movers are two college students who arrive with a rented van, and they've quoted me for three hours of work, including taking apart my old desk. I donated the printer and the filing cabinet, but my monitor and keyboard have moved to the dining table, where they will probably stay forever. Eli's grandmother bought him a rug with a road pattern for the floor, and he's already declared it his favorite thing in the house.

What should I do with the dresser?

A) Leave it in the old nursery for now and put what he needs for tonight in a basket
B) Wait until my husband is home tonight and then decide
C) Move it into his room now against the wall and fill the drawers with his clothes

I'm buying a convertible car seat for my eight-month-old and found a listing for the same brand we looked at in the store, thirty dollars versus about one hundred eighty new. It looks clean, the straps are intact, and the label shows it hasn't expired. The seller says it was in her car during a rear-end collision last spring, when the airbags went off.

Money is tight this month because we're paying for a new roof, and the quote came in higher than the estimate we got in the spring. My husband has picked up extra weekend shifts, and I've been selling outgrown baby clothes online to cover the gap. The roofers start Monday and expect to be done in four days if the weather holds, which means we'll have a lot of noise and a dumpster in the driveway. Our baby is starting to pull himself up on the furniture and has two teeth coming in, so he's not sleeping well. My mother has offered to chip in for a few things, but I'd rather not ask her unless I have to. The seller lives about fifteen minutes away and can meet this evening, and she says another buyer has asked about it.

I'd like to get this sorted today. What should I do?

A) Buy it for thirty dollars today and install it tonight
B) Buy a new entry-level seat for around seventy-five dollars
C) Hold off on deciding until I've talked it over with my husband

My daughter Maya is in second grade and has a peanut allergy that her allergist confirmed two years ago. She carries an epinephrine pen in her backpack, and her class has a field trip to the science museum on Friday. The caterer's menu says every child gets a peanut-butter-and-jelly sandwich in the boxed lunch.

The permission slip is due back tomorrow morning, and the teacher has asked for volunteers to chaperone, though I can't get time off from work that day. Maya is thrilled about the trip: she has been talking about the planetarium show for two weeks and has already told us which exhibits she wants to see first. The class is going by bus, leaving at nine and returning around two-thirty, and the teacher wants every child to wear a labeled name tag and a bright shirt. We've been working on her reading, and she wants to write a short report afterward with drawings of the dinosaur bones. My husband's mother is visiting this weekend and already bought her a new notebook for the occasion. The school sends home a lot of paperwork, and our fridge door is covered with permission slips, lunch calendars and a flyer for the spring concert. I don't want Maya to feel singled out, because last year she asked me why she always had to eat something different.

She wants to eat with her friends. What should I do?

A) Pack her own lunch and send it with her
B) Sign the slip and let her eat the boxed lunch with the class
C) Hold off on signing until I've talked to her teacher tomorrow morning

We're driving from Phoenix to San Diego with our one-year-old on Sunday, and I want to arrive in time for a barbecue at 6 with friends. The forecast for the desert stretch is 108 degrees in the afternoon. The car's air conditioning stopped working last week and hasn't been repaired.

The barbecue is at our friends' new house near the water, and they have been planning it for weeks. They bought a smoker and a lot of ribs, and the host has texted three times to ask about dietary restrictions, even though we've told him none of us have any. Our son has been fussy about car rides, but he usually naps after the first hour if we have his stuffed giraffe and the right playlist. I've packed the diaper bag, two changes of clothes, a cooler with his snacks and a travel crib for the hotel stay we've booked afterward. My husband is trying to fit our suitcases and the stroller into the trunk, and it looks like a game of Tetris that he's losing. We have also promised to bring a pie, which I haven't baked yet. The drive is about five and a half hours without stops, and with a baby, we always stop at least twice, so I'd planned to leave at eleven to be safe on time.

What should we do about the drive?

A) Leave at 4 am and plan a long midday break at a hotel along the way
B) Hold off on deciding until we've talked it through tonight
C) Leave at 11 as planned and make our usual two stops

Where should I leave the bottle?

A) Keep it in the high kitchen cabinet and take it after breakfast
B) Leave it on the nightstand where I can reach it half-asleep
